en: Chapter 1:
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed Noble Kurukullā! In this tantra born of Tārā, which has been lost, departed, and vanished, [this is] the great ocean of yoga.
The great Ādhitantra named Tārārṇava has been lost; therefore, this ritual manual (kalpa) is presented once again. // 1 //

Having extracted from the tantras and their extensive commentaries the yogas and practical applications for the sake of many beings, Lokeśvara spoke this ritual manual: "Let all the bodhisattvas indeed listen! (2)

Having observed today that this world, though performing what is beneficial for all people, is without refuge and subject to the suffering of the three types of misery, you should grasp this method with great reverence. (3)
This ritual manual (kalpa) has been composed by all these hosts of Buddhas for the sake of pacifying the conceptual constructions of the world;
it was spoken at the Śrīpotala mountain by Mañjuśrī, the victorious bearer of the lotus. 4.

This continuous sequence of Dharma verses was indeed heard by Viṣkambhin, Sāgarabuddhi, Maitreya and his foremost followers, and by all the assemblies; it was rejoiced in and even venerated with their heads bowed. // 5 //
Cultivated by the sons of all the Victors, he was praised with excellent songs and musical instruments,
and honored with various dances by yakṣas, māras, and the world-protectors.

The lords of the bears and those with nooses in their hands who dwell upon the waves of the ocean, the serpent maidens skilled in side-long glances, the guardians of the underworld, and the daughters of the gods and *siddhas*—[all these attend you]. (7)

The queens of the Gandharvas, those longing for fine fragrances, the wives of Vidyādharas and Kinnaras, the women of the Yakṣas, and the sons and grandsons of the Mountain—these all speak thus: "We are without refuge; we belong to you. (8)

For he is indeed the protector of this world who is without a protector; by him, within this teaching of the Buddha, there is a great and marvelous happiness for all beings, having heard the words of this assembly, O Protector. (9)
The King of Mantras, which brings about subjugation, spoke it himself; all those women, having heard this sovereign mantra, attained the bliss of the Buddha.
As many as several tens of millions of them, emitting their vital essence, longed intensely for perfect equanimity.
They gaze with sidelong glances; their feet stumble as they fall to the ground;
they emit semen and twist in passion. // 11 //
Having seen this, the Lord spoke these timely words to the beautiful celestial maidens:
"The Kurukullā mantra, which brings people under one's control, is to be written upon a cloth that has been consecrated by that mantra. (12)
Having heard this, the Blessed One, the Lord of the World in the three realms, proclaimed the ritual action.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the ritual for the cloth-painting (paṭa) of Kurukullā, by the mere drawing of which the practitioner shall attain accomplishment. // 14 //
I shall determine by which painter, on which lunar day, and at what time this was done, according to the account arising from Tāra.
She whose eyes are copper-red, whose hands and feet are likewise red,
and whose shanks are like those of an elephant or a deer— by him Tāriṇī should be painted.
In the first month of spring, on the eighth day of Aśoka, at the time of half a watch (sārdhapraharavelā), Tāriṇī should indeed be drawn upon the eyes. 17.
He should eat the three sweets and avoid fish; he should abstain from liquor and meat, always wear red garments, and be anointed with red perfumes. (18)
Having generated a mind of loving-kindness, bathing in the morning at a temple of Śiva and changing his clothes three times, he should draw the Vaśakāriṇī [mantra-diagram]. (19)
She has one face, large eyes, and four arms; she resembles saffron in color, is sixteen years of age, is full of amorous grace, and is proud with the illusory power of a woman.
The cloth should be made from thread spun by a young cowherd girl who has subsisted only on milk, and it should be woven by a weaver who has likewise subsisted only on milk. // 21 //

Seated upon a red lotus throne, wearing a red bodice and upper garment, and adorned with a red crown and earrings; she grants the gesture of fearlessness with her first right hand, holds an arrow drawn to the string with the second, carries a bow in her first left hand, and holds a red utpala lotus with the second; she wears a crown inscribed with the syllable *Āḥ* and dwells within the mountain cave of Kurukullā. (22)

Upon Kurukullā is Rāhu; above him is Kāma together with his consort; above Kāma is a lunar disc, and upon that is a seat of red lotuses. Having brought the Blessed Lady to completion there, adorned with all varieties of artistic splendor, and having consecrated the cloth painting, one should perform eighteen offerings before that painting and recite the mantra from the eighth day of the bright fortnight until the full moon. This is done with this Heart-mantra of Tārā. (23)
With the mantra: Oṃ Kurukulle hrīḥ hūṃ svāhā. // 24 //

Then, having performed the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) for one hundred thousand [recitations], again—at the festival of the Buddha on a lunar day in either the month of Kārttika, Mādhava, or Āṣāḍha—one should bathe in the morning, observe the *poṣadha* vows, and present all offerings. Having given food to the community of disciples (*śrāvakasaṅgha*), one should afterwards feed the assembly (*gaṇa*) devoted to the Mantra Mahāyāna. Having requested them according to their accomplishment and given them a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), with the upper robe draped over one shoulder and the right knee placed upon the ground, one should pay homage to and ask forgiveness from both the community of disciples and the assembly devoted to the Mantra Mahāyāna. Then, approaching the place where the Blessed Lady has been brought down onto the cloth-painting (*paṭa*), the Vidyādhara, endowed with meditative concentration, should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for the sake of accomplishment. 25.
By one part wisdom increases; by another part he becomes a subjugator;
and by the third part alone, the man becomes an extractor of poison. (26)
He shall be honored by the entire world, even by women who are arrogant with pride;
through the power of practice, that master of mantras enjoys beautiful women according to his desire. (27)
By his name alone, even the most virulent poisons depart; the serpents become like rays from the hood of the Lord of Nagas, and turn into harmless fish.
Those endowed with the power of speech, through the efficacy of their recitation, render even learned men—though they be arrogant in their strength of knowledge—speechless. // 28 //

The most eminent among those who know mantras, having realized the pleasures of sovereignty within his mind, triumphs through the power of his spells over the Vidyādharas— who are mounted on the backs of elephants and horses and whose necks are concealed by a retinue of mature women— as he prepares to enjoy those very pleasures.
Having conquered through mantras Rati from Kāma, Girijā from Giriśa, Śrī from Nārāyaṇa, Śacī from Akhaṇḍalaka, the pure Gīśvarī from Vācaspati, and even Lakṣmī from Dharaṇīdhara; || 30 ||

With his mind fixed upon various treasures, wealth, earrings, gold, silver, clothing, and all such kinds of riches, he who possesses the mantra and meditates upon the Blessed Lady draws everything without exception toward himself with his mind and enjoys it. (31)
One draws forth from the king the fruit of sovereignty, and from the tree the water that has reached the rivers, streams, and oceans;
endowed with mantras, one drinks and eats what is purified by mantras—for indeed, without mantra, the attainment of enjoyments is never mastered.

Then the minister, by the audacity of his own mantra-power, drew forth wild elephants born from the lineage of excellent horses, hooded serpents endowed with enjoyments yet arrogant with venom, as well as crocodiles, rhinoceroses, bears, tigers, and even gaṇḍakas.
If that accomplished master of mantra beholds him with a gaze of loving-kindness, his eyes free from wonder, he ascends [to the celestial realm]. // 34 //

If that minister gazes upon the worlds here with a compassionate eye, she rescues the entire world from the treacherous and crooked suffering of separation and brings about peace; for Tārā becomes a wish-fulfilling gem for the welfare of the world. (35)
Having conquered the Māras, he would rain down a shower of treasures; having brought forth the silver from the foot of Mount Kalpa, he would give it to the people.
Having drawn out all the wealth belonging to the Lord of Riches (Kubera), he would bring it to fruition for the benefit of the entire world. (36)
Likewise, for the sake of all those who are miserable, she may become clothing, a seat, a house, or even a canopy here in this world;
and in times of calamity, she becomes a bridge that removes all misfortunes, like a bridge for ruined merchants in the midst of the ocean. (37)
The yogi should meditate on that Tārā; first, he should act as if he were suffering.
By worshipping her for even a single day, a man shall obtain food. (38)
In the second [period], one will obtain clothing; thereafter, there will be union with women;
and then, one will enjoy betel-leaf as desired, without even having to ask for it. (39)
If a celibate student should consume a maiden born of the gods, or one who is intent on the slaughter of sentient beings, he will not attain success here in this teaching. (40)
Having become one who delights in the ten virtues and has made the Mahāyāna his sole intention, he enjoys vast accomplishment, just as Vajradharma spoke. // 41 //
The First Chapter: The Ritual for Unfurling the Cloth. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that by which the principles of reality (dharmatās) are satisfied.
Through the practice of the worship of Dharma, the Dharmadhātu itself shall become manifest. // 1 //
Now, therefore, follows the method for accomplishing the wish-fulfilling tree.
One should visualize the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṛkṣa) as arisen from the syllable VṚṂ;
through the transformation of the blue lotus, one should visualize the tree with the left hand. // 2 //

Meditating that the Lord of Wealth (Dhaneśvara) was raining down a great shower of various riches from the vault of the sky to fulfill the hopes of those who seek them, [he offered the oblation]. // 3 //
Having drawn in the sentient beings dwelling in the four continents with the ray of light from the mind, one should always bestow upon them gifts consisting of the seven precious jewels. (4)
The great jewel of the counselor, the oceanic jewel, the jewel of a woman, the jewel of a horse, and likewise the jewel of a sword. // 5 //
One should mentally create elephant-jewels and other such jewels for the Buddhas;
likewise, one should create a jewel of a woman, beautifully adorned, possessing various forms and playful grace.
One who desires the fruit of Buddhahood should mentally offer [these] to the Buddhas;
by this, the Vidyādhara attains the state of all-encompassing Buddhahood. // 7 //
One who desires the fruit of Buddhahood should respectfully offer to the Buddhas the Lord of Wealth, the Guide, who is filled with a great treasury. (8)
In this way, one should respectfully renounce other jewels;
by embracing the state of Vajradharma, one shall become a benefactor of all sentient beings. 9.
The Sadhana of the Kalpavṛkṣa (Wish-fulfilling Tree).
Through the mind, all buddhahood is attained; by the mind alone one is liberated.
Through the mind one is released from bondage, and through the mind one becomes possessed of liberation. // 10 //
Apart from the mind, no other state of things is perceived; for it is the mind that constitutes Buddhahood, all spiritual accomplishments, and indeed all other manifestations. (11)
But those moving vessels that arise from the primary elements and their derivatives are known by the wise ones free from outflows as being "mere cognition. (12)
Therefore, with every effort, one should polish the mirror of the mind;
in this way, innate and adventitious defects will be gradually abandoned. (13)
Having visualized the moon of the mind, which is stainless, radiant as the full moon, and arisen from the primordial vowel, one should place the seed-syllable upon it. // 14 //
And the fourth of the sibilants (ūṣman), situated above the color of fire, is joined with the vowel *ī* and adorned with two spaces (*ākāśa*). // 15 //
Having made the world stainless with his variegated rays, and having purified the Sahā world-system and the other realms, he went to Mount Kurukulla. (16)
Having thus exhorted Tārā and caused her to be brought forth, the wise one should place her in front and emanate great clouds of offerings from that seed-syllable. (17)
With collections of flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, and food offerings, as well as with dances, garlands, songs, instrumental music, and other forms of worship; (18)
The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds; I rejoice in the merit of the world; I set my mind upon the enlightenment of a Buddha. (19)
This mantra should be recited three times, and then one should say, "May [the offense] be forgiven.
At that time, the mind should again be established in the dwelling of loving-kindness.
Having generated a mind of compassion, one should bring forth a mind of joy;
thereafter, one remains equanimous toward everything through the established principle that all is mind-only.
One should again make the mind empty in order to abandon ordinary forms; the five aggregates, when consumed by the fire of emptiness, do not arise again. (22)
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness.
For a moment, one should practice the yoga of emptiness to allow the mind to rest. (23)
Recalling his former vow, he should again remember the seed-syllable:
"I have deceived those beings who have attained final nirvāṇa. (24)
Thinking, "How shall I deliver them from the bottomless ocean of existence? one filled with compassion should abandon the motionless state of emptiness. (25)
One generates with the mind a consciousness consisting of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu); from the empowerment of the Buddha, there arises the seed known as the utpala lotus. (26)
Upon the lotus is the lunar disc, which arises from the sound of the vowel *a*; upon that moon is the seed-syllable, and from it rays of light radiate forth. (27)
By those [rays], all world-systems without exception are to be purified as objects of meditation;
likewise, all the millions of Buddhas are to be purified and awakened by means of rays of light. // 28 //
One should meditate on them entering with seed-syllables; then the arising of the *tāra* occurs.
The goddess is red-colored, holding weapons, and adorned with all ornaments. (29)
Having attained the form of the commitment (*samayamūrti*), one should summon the wisdom-wheel (*jñānacakra*).
The wisdom-wheel, instantly perfected in its appearance, stands before one. (30)
One should enter the path of bliss through the yoga of the *samayamudrā*;
when the two hands are joined in *añjali* with the fleshy parts [of the palms] bent inward. (31)
A needle is formed by making the two index fingers long; the two ring fingers are placed in the middle of the needle;
the two middle fingers are joined like creepers; and the two thumbs are positioned below. (32)
With this, one should bind the pledge; with this, one should cause [the disciple] to enter the maṇḍala.
Then, the adept, reciting the verse "Then one should request consecration from the Buddhas," should pray for the empowerment. 33.
Just as the great festival was bestowed upon the Buddhas by Bodhivajra, so too, for the sake of my protection, O Khavajra, grant it to me today! (34)
Those great beings bestow upon the king a kingdom known as "consecration," just like the flower-consecration of a monarch, by means of the five [consorts] beginning with Locanā. (35)
I bestow the great vajra consecration, honored by the three realms, which arises from the source of the three secrets of all the Buddhas. // 36 //
Through the empowerment of the Buddhas, Tārā becomes the Crest-Jewel of the Dharma, illuminating the three worlds with the radiance of her red and variegated light. (37)
But having obtained the jewel of consecration, one should accomplish all siddhis for half a year through firm possession, according to the previously stated ritual procedure. (38)

Having offered a bali-oblation at the three junctions of the day with this mantra, using sugar, flour-cakes, and other such items according to the prescribed rite, one shall obtain the knowledge of dreams. (39)
The sword, the accomplishment of the netherworld, invisibility, alchemy, invisibility, the power of moving through the sky, as well as foot-ointment and collyrium.
Through a dream, self-accomplished recognition arises spontaneously;
one should not strive for minor accomplishments if one is devoted to the Tārās.

Endowed with the practice of recitation and meditative cultivation, one may achieve the status of a universal monarch, kingship, the state of Indra, or even universal sovereignty as if in a dream. (42)
At the end of six months, for one month, the practitioner should recite throughout the entire night;
having formed the utpala mudrā, he should continue until the mudrā blazes forth in an instant.
By the power of that mudrā, Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, Rudra, and the others, together with their wives, are drawn forth and arrive, brought under control. // 44 //
From that time forth, he became perfected as the self of all, free from the latent impressions of saṃsāra,
just as a lotus is unsullied by the defects of mud or water.
Just as molten metal, when touched [by another], does not remain separate but attains unity,
so too do the minds of the perfected ones attain omniscience.
Just as base metal becomes a treasure when touched by a perfected alchemist’s elixir, so too do practitioners of mantra become the bodies of Buddhas when touched by the elixirs of mantra. 47.
They attain the lordship of the thirty-three gods and become great lords of the triple world;
born into the lineage of the Buddhas, they set the wheel of Dharma in motion. // 48 //
They undergo births, go forth into homelessness, and approach the seat of awakening; they practice difficult austerities and remain mindful of their state as Buddhas. (49)
The manifestation of the descent from heaven, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, the attainment of final nirvāṇa, and likewise the journey to the cremation ground. // 50 //
Having abandoned the physical elements within the three worlds, the Victors depart from their bodies of enjoyment and form,
and return once more to the Pure Abodes, having left behind their emanation bodies.
Having set in motion the Dharma-body through the sequence of books, paintings, and so forth, that very mantra is accomplished; it was spoken by that Buddha. (52)
The Second Chapter: The Ritual Manual for the Realization of Kurukullā.
Chapter Three.

Then all those bodhisattvas, having reflected within their own minds upon their own thoughts, spoke thus to the great bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi: "Vajrapāṇi, how is it that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones—who possess a vajra-body, a body of the *dharmadhātu*, and an indestructible body—perform the act of passing away (*kālakriyā*) in some region of the earth? Then Vajrapāṇi said to those bodhisattvas: "O bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, do not speak in this way. How can it be that the Buddhas—who possess a vajra-body, an indestructible body, and a body of the *dharmadhātu*—perform the act of passing away in some region of the earth? Then Vajrapāṇi said: "In this regard, O bodhisattvas, listen: when the Blessed One passed into final nirvāṇa (*parinirvṛta*), he went to Sukhāvatī. (1)

Then the Bodhisattvas asked: "Vajrapāṇi, do the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, go to Sukhāvatī after abandoning the body? He replied: "Noble sons, they go to Sukhāvatī by means of the *saṃbhogakāya* after abandoning the *nirmāṇakāya*. The Bodhisattvas said: "In that case, Vajrapāṇi, how is it that they go having abandoned the body? Vajrapāṇi said: "It is just as some illusory person (*māyāvī puruṣa*), for the sake of a certain purpose, might manifest an illusion and thereby accomplish that purpose. (2)
Likewise, Buddhas who had previously attained perfection took on birth once again for the sake of favoring sentient beings when a Cakravartin had passed into nirvāṇa. // 3 //
When there are no Buddhas here, then a wheel-turning monarch may appear;
yet the world is never produced devoid of both.
Having approached the world of those to be trained and having disciplined them, the Buddhas, the supreme among bipeds,
remained for eighty years and then departed for the abode of the Victors.
Having abandoned the Buddha-māyā, they remain in Sukhāvatī, the abode of the Jinas, attached to the bliss of great tranquility in the form of bliss. // 6 //
The sages consider the mind to be an eternal, unitary experiencer and agent;
such is its nature, and it is not held to be truly momentary or empty. (7)
For those ruined by the grasping at a self and constantly longing for the notion of permanence, the Victors abandoned their bodies in order to lead them into the realization of impermanence. (8)
For those whose minds are omniscient and who realize the intrinsic nature of all phenomena,
there exists no certainty whatsoever as to what is possible or what is impossible.
Relying upon conventional truth, the Dharma teachings of the Buddhas proceed like the sky for those to be trained, amidst excellent assemblies and so forth. (10)
The arising of a Buddha does not exist in reality, nor indeed does the destruction of a Buddha;
when all have become of one single flavor, there is neither arising nor passing away.
They are of a single form with the dharmadhātu, free from the five obscurations;
they abide in the nature of reality by way of their profound and sublime form. // 12 //
They have not attained either existence or non-existence, because both are impossible;
from the very beginning they lack intrinsic nature, being neither ceased nor yet to come into being. (13)

The Bodhisattvas asked: “Vajrapāṇi, how is it that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones who rule over the three realms, are neither arisen nor ceased? Vajrapāṇi replied: “Bodhisattvas, what do you think? Is that which is the Buddha existent or non-existent? The Bodhisattvas replied: “Vajrapāṇi, the Buddhas are neither existent nor non-existent. (14)
Vajrapāṇi said:
"That which is unborn is not to be born, nor is there an arising for that which has already been born.
Therefore, in the ultimate analysis, all things are unarisen from the very beginning. (15)
Thus, those who have died are not to die again, nor is there death for the immortal;
there is no stability for the unstable, nor is there stability for that which is already stable. (16)
If the unborn were to undergo destruction, or if the unborn were to arise again, then the destruction and arising of a rabbit's horn would occur. (17)
If birth were the arising of what already exists, it would be the re-emergence of what has already been born;
and if there were the production of even that which does not exist, then there would be the birth of the son of a barren woman. (18)
Therefore, the wise know that all this—ignorance, the three characteristics of formative forces, and the world endowed with the five aggregates—is merely a matter of conventional appearance. (19)
By this principle, it follows that the Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, and the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have entered final nirvana. // 20 //
The bodhisattvas said:
How are the mudrās? How are the mantras? How is the meditation on the maṇḍala? And how are the accomplishments accomplished, given that all things are characterized by non-arising? (21)
Vajrapāṇi said:
For things arise dependently;
for accomplishments arise dependently upon mantras, mudrās, and so forth. // 22 //

Even the accomplishments (siddhis) belonging to the Buddha, as well as the perfections (pāramitās), and even Buddhahood and the state of Vajrasattva—one should establish these through conventional reality alone. (23)
The Third Chapter: The Ritual Manual for the Bodhicitta of Kurukullā.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of the ritual procedure for the recitation of the mantra.
By the mere knowledge of which, the practitioner shall attain accomplishment. // 1 //
One should bring others under control with coral; the lotus-seed (puṣkara) is for the destruction of poison;
through crystal, wisdom increases—one should employ these three in the three types of rites. // 2 //

By means of purification of the womb, having kindled a fire with *aśoka* wood in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) shaped like an *aśvattha* leaf, one should offer eight hundred red lotuses, anointed with the three sweets, according to the ritual procedure using the root mantra and the fire from a dancer’s house. (3)

Afterwards, the yantra is prepared: having drawn a triangular maṇḍala on a cloth stained with menstrual blood, one should write in the center the names of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) and the practitioner (sādhaka), joined with the word "codaka" and the formula "May so-and-so be brought under my control. Then, having interlaced [the names] with the root mantra, one should draw it using lac juice mixed with the blood from the ring finger of the left hand, along with camphor, saffron, musk, and other pigments. // 4 //

For the increase of wisdom, having kindled a fire in that very pit with wood from the *arka* and *karavīra* trees, one should offer ten thousand oblations of *aṭarūṣaka* leaves or pieces of *vacā* using the sacrificial fire of a Brahmin. // 5 //

For the destruction of poison, one should kindle a fire in that very same sacrificial pit with sandalwood fuel and offer ten thousand *piṇḍatagara* flowers as oblations. Thereupon, one becomes a remover of all poisons; one dispels the suffering of those afflicted by various diseases and brings about peace. This is the ritual procedure for the *Garuḍa*. 6.
Whatever women are known to exist along the delightful paths of the three realms,
one may enjoy them all through the application of the fire-offering mantra.
Through the observation of passion, loving-kindness is brought forth; by that mind, [the world] is brought under control.
Having brought the entire world under control, one should establish it in the awakening of a Buddha. // 8 //
Thus ends the procedure for subjugation.
That which is called the knowledge of all aspects cannot be attained without wisdom;
therefore, one who desires to attain it should cultivate sharp wisdom. (9)
Through the practice of fire-offerings and mantra-recitation.
Wisdom that discerns all phenomena, pure and radiating light—that indeed is the perfection of wisdom; by means of it, the yogi is liberated. (10)
The procedure for increasing wisdom.
The wise man should consume the leaves called *gṛha*, *ṣaṣṭhī*, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, as well as *brahmāṇī* and *māgadhī*, along with honey.
The Tantra for Increasing Wisdom.
Ghee, the root of *tagara*, and likewise the *cakrāṅkita* plant, remove poison through an application as an ointment or by drinking it when there is a bite from fangs. // 12 //
The Tantra for the Destruction of Poison.
The Jārī, Caṇḍālikā, Snehamallī, Svaśukraka, Mṛtā, and Udarakīṭā bring others under one's control when consumed. (13)
The tantra of subjugation.
Through the extraction of poison, there is peace for the world; through the increase of wisdom, Buddhahood is attained;
and by performing the rite of subjugation, one brings about the turning of the Wheel of Dharma in an instant. (14)
There is no other means in the Mahāyāna for the accomplishment of the welfare of oneself and others; this vidyā, when uttered but once, produces immediate conviction. (15)
The syllable *hrīḥ*, placed upon the parasol of passion, causes the flow [of fluids] for women;

that same syllable on the tongue generates awakening, and in the center of the heart as well. When meditated upon for those who have been bitten, this beautiful, sacred syllable (*dharmākṣara*) is the remover of poison.
The heart-mantra of Tārā, which conquers the three worlds, should be known by those endowed with compassion. (16)

Through the complete elimination of faults in speech, it is declared that there is an increase in wisdom; through the removal of faults of the mind, one becomes a subduer who casts away the faults of existence. For this entire world, being seized by unwholesome states, would not attain accomplishment.
Therefore, O sons of the Conqueror, being well-disposed toward our welfare, you should censure what is unwholesome right here. // 17 //
Through the specific binding of mudrās, the defects born of the body indeed go to destruction;

for those whose tongues have been cleansed by mantra, the defects born of speech and those born of the mind [are destroyed] through meditation practiced by those whose minds are seated in dhyāna. Therefore, O people, have faith!
For the Buddhas abide in a state of complete composure regarding body, speech, and mind. // 18 //
With eyes that behold the absence of the spread of evil, through compassion he becomes a king of the three worlds;
by giving, he possesses superior merit and power like the Lord of Wealth (Kubera); through vigor, he becomes a ruler of mortals;
and by removing laziness, the skillful one does not experience even the slightest suffering born of hell.
O sons of the Buddha, practice compassion and the conduct of giving wealth and valor! 19 //
With a pure heart through the power of constant meditation, one beholds the Buddhas in the sky;
one should always perceive oneself as being attended by the Tathāgatas even in dreams.
The wise, at the time of death, travel to the various celestial palaces of the Buddhas and to Mount Meru.
Those whose nature is compassion behold [them], while those in hell behold the city of sin.
Now follows the Viśuddhitantra.
Where there is desire, there is poison; therein alone does the intellect abide.
For this very reason, how indeed can the Mistress of Speech (Vāgīśā) be considered Pāṇḍarā? 21.
That very goddess, who removes poison, abides in the state of Hayagrīva;
arisen from the state of Rāgavajra, she brings the three worlds under her control. // 22 //
The accomplishment of the Rāgakula Tantra.
Now, there is also another application.
Having drawn a triangular maṇḍala and another triangle within it,
the skillful practitioner should write the syllables beginning with Oṃ, starting from the eastern direction.
One should write the six seed-syllables in the six corners and the seed-syllable of Dharma in the center;
having placed it within the syllable *phuḥ*, one should write it upon the lintel of the doorway.
The Tantra of the Subduing of Serpents.

Now, there is another application for bringing about the good fortune of women: having fashioned a seven-petaled lotus, the seven syllables should be applied therein. In its pericarp, one should write the name of the woman to be accomplished, interspersed with two *hrīḥ* syllables, according to the procedure for subjugation (*vaśya*). Having placed this on birch bark or on a cloth from a menstruating woman, and having fastened it to the arm, one should cause her to wear it. // 25 //
A husband may become subject to his wives, or kings to their servants;
one who is pure and well-purified should recite this mantra.
This is the ritual procedure for the tantra of subjugation.
Now follows the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*).
Having fashioned a four-petaled lotus, one should then draw a moon in the center; and in the east one should draw an arrow, while in the south one should likewise draw a bow. (27)
One should draw the hand granting fearlessness (abhayapāṇi) in the west and the utpala lotus in the north;
one should then encircle the afflicted person within the moon with the seven seed-syllables.
Having drawn this wheel, which is surrounded on the outside and adorned with a garland of lotuses, upon a birch-bark leaf, one should wear it upon one's own arm. 29.
There is eternal protection for children, the elderly, and the young.
The accomplishment of the protective tantras.

Now, one who desires to become a lord should draw a citron fruit (*bījapūraka*) and, in its center, draw a bow. Upon the bow, he should draw a lotus bud in the form of a jewel. In the center of the lotus bud, he should write the syllable *jrūṃ* encircled by the seven-syllable mantra. Having written this on a leaf of gold, he should place it upon the roof of his house. Having surrounded it externally with a garland of lotuses, on the eighth day of the twelfth month, he should lower it [into water] with a jar filled with the five jewels, bathe it, worship it, and recite the mantra one hundred times. Within one year, he becomes equal to Dhanada (Kubera). He should also cause him to wear such a magical spell (*vidyā*). // 30 //
Now, there is another application as well:

On a Tuesday at midday, having obtained a painted cowrie shell, one should begin by performing worship with the mantra of Kurukullā recited eight hundred times. Having bathed it on the twelfth and eighth lunar days, one should wrap it in a cloth and wear it on the arm; one will become a great lord of wealth. Placing that cowrie shell in the palm of the hand, one should recite the mantra ten million times; one will achieve victory in gambling. Having placed that cowrie shell in a vessel, one should bury it in the ground; one obtains one *kārṣāpaṇa* every day. // 31 //
The Tantra of the Accomplishment of Wealth, the Accomplishment of Sovereignty, and the Fruit of Success in Winning at Dice.
The fourth ritual manual of Kurukullā is completed.
Chapter Five:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of the mandala, by the mere sight of whose colored powders one may swiftly attain the state of Buddhahood. (1)
It is square, with four gates, adorned with four archways;
there, in the center, one should draw the goddess in the form of a vulva, beautifully colored.
One should draw an arrow in the east, and a bow in the south;
in the west, a hand in the gesture of fearlessness, and likewise a lotus in the north.
In all the corner sections, there are four [deities] beginning with Vajracakra;
they wear red garments as upper cloths and possess red ornaments. // 4 //
And having bound the disciple's face with a red cloth, one should cause him to enter. // 5 //

Having bound the Sattvavajrī mudrā with this [mantra], one should have the casting of flowers upon the wheel. Having uttered "pratīccha vajra hoḥ," one should reveal the maṇḍala. If it falls in the center, it is excellent. If it falls on the arrow, one becomes fit for the rite of subjugation (*vaśyakarma*). If it falls on the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), one should teach the removal of poison. If it falls on the lotus, one should teach the increase of wisdom (*prajñā*). If it falls on the bow, one should teach the knowledge of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). Having caused him to enter, one should speak thus: "You must not speak of this supreme secret of all the Tathāgatas before anyone who has not entered the maṇḍala. Lest your samaya be violated; by failing to avoid misfortune, you will die and fall into hell. // 6 //
Thereafter, one should grant the pledges (*samaya*) concerning the Three Jewels and so forth; such is the extensive tantra. Having granted the pledges... // 7 //
Then, having extracted that great blood from the hearts of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and those who practice the supreme conduct of mantras, you should drink it. 8.
If you transgress the great covenant of the King of Dharma in my presence, you must not treat with contempt me, the protector of the teaching of the Dharma. // 9 //
One should always wear red garments, bind on a red garland, apply red perfumes and unguents, and adorn oneself with red jewels. (10)
The mantra practitioner, with a red heart and a red mind, should meditate;
or else, he should fashion the city out of vermilion, red ochre, or colored powders.
Or with powders of cinnabar, or with saffron and red sandalwood, or even with molten coral mixed with karketana dust.
Whether at home or likewise during the consecration of a maṇḍala and so forth, everything should be made red, signifying the saffron robes of a Buddha. // 13 //
Living beings must not be killed by you; false speech must not be uttered;
what is not given must not be taken by you; and the wives of others must not be pursued.
Bodily action is of three kinds, while vocal action is fourfold; they say mental action is threefold—abandon these unwholesome [actions], O you! (15)

The fourfold gift—of the Dharma, material goods, loving-kindness, and fearlessness—should always be given by you through the practice of meditative concentration until all things have ceased to exist. 16.
One should constantly train in the four means of attraction, as well as the ten perfections, the stages, the powers, and the masteries. (17)
Women must not be disregarded, especially one named Tārā;
even a householder who is a minister should never marry such a woman.
In the city, the market town, the village, and the countryside wherever the Tāriṇī [is present],
especially on the main road, at the crossroads, along the street, and at the junctions.
One should constantly pay homage to that place, describe it, and honor it;
having established oneself in that place, one should perform the practice of the mantras and so forth. (20)
But when a woman named Tārā, who is reddish-fair and has beautiful eyes, is seen, the yogin should respectfully offer her mental salutation. (21)
The practitioner should never step over the bandhūka, the pomegranate flower, the karavīra, the javā, nor any other red flowers. (22)
Having thus bestowed the vow of restraint, he [should bathe] the pure disciple with divine water, purified by the waters of the mantra, and with the water from the four jars.
The preceptor should perform the ablution consecutively with the mudrās of the arrow, the bow, and so forth;
first with the arrow-vessel, and second with the bow.
The third [is marked] with an *abhaya* hand and a lotus; the fourth is as that of the Lion of the Śākyas, together with the Buddhas and their sons who hold the vajra. (25)
Just as you were consecrated with the royal empowerment, so have you been consecrated by me;
indeed, this very day you have attained all-buddhahood within the mandala.
Indeed, upon seeing these dust particles, the Buddhas become exceedingly serene;
for you there shall be no death, no disease, no sorrow, and no poverty. (27)
But you have attained perfect awakening by means of this Great Pure Vehicle, having made [beings] vessels for the True Dharma through the consecration of the four arrows and so forth. (28)
The secret gnoses should be bestowed upon the disciple according to the sequence of rites;
the divine mandala has been taught, empowered by all the Buddhas. (29)
It is square, with four gates, adorned with four archways,
decorated with strings and half-strings of pearls, and beautified by eight pillars.
In its corner, one should draw a vajra garlanded with jewels and moonbeams; and in the center, one should also draw a wheel garlanded with eight vajras and moonbeams. // 31 //
Above the wheel, one should draw a vajra adorned with a garland of vajras, blazing and as stainless as the full moon with its rays like those of the autumnal moon. (32)
And eight jars should be placed, filled with the five great medicinal herbs, adorned with the five grains, the five jewels, and the five sprouts. // 33 //
Filled with the five nectars and wrapped in a pair of garments, their limbs smeared with white sandalwood paste and adorned with flower garlands. // 34 //
And they were beautifully adorned with garlands of lamps and various kinds of edible food offerings.

Then, having consecrated the victory flask (*vijayakalaśa*) one hundred and eight times with mantras, and having adorned it with the five great medicinal herbs, the five jewels of rice, and the five colors—white, black, red, yellow, and green—and having established and honored it;
[one should prepare] a canopy spread out and adorned with various banners, hung with garlands of flowers, fragrant, and perfumed with incense. (36)
One should cause the disciple to enter there with his face veiled by a pair of garments;
then, one should give him a tooth-stick for the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin. (37)

Having consecrated all the ritual implements according to the prescribed sequence with the mantra "Oṃ mārīcyai svāhā," [one should offer] those whose limbs are smeared with sandalwood paste and adorned with garlands and strings of flowers. (38)

In that regard, first one should teach the secret practice of summoning the *nāgas*. Homage to the Three Jewels! Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas! Homage to the eight classes of *pudgalas*! Homage to all the millions of Buddhas! It is as follows: Oṃ hrīḥ hrīḥ hrīḥ! To all the *nāgas* of the Ananta family, the Vāsuki family, the Takṣaka family, the Śaṅkhapāla family, the Karkoṭaka family, the Padma family, the Mahāpadma family, the Kulika family, the Varāha family, the Puṇḍarīka family, the Ghana family, the Megha family, the Jalada family, the Jaladhara family, the Jīmūta family, the Saṃvarta family, the Vasanta family, the Airāvata family, the Kumuda family, the Kahlāra family, and the Saugandhika family: strike, strike with the arrow! Bind, bind with the bow! Strike, strike with the lotus! Grant fearlessness to those who are afraid! Make it rain like a cloud at the time of universal destruction! Subjugate those *nāgas*, subjugate them! *Kuru kuru phuḥ kulāpaya kulāpaya phuḥ phuḥ!* Oṃ Kurukulle hrīḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā phaṭ! Having made a mandala with wild cow dung using this mantra, and having drawn an eight-petaled lotus with sandalwood according to the ritual rules, one should place the eight *nāgas* beginning with Ananta in the petals starting from the east. Under the Rohiṇī asterism, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times while fumigating the *nāgas* with sugar and *guggulu* resin. Afterwards, one should worship them; then they will rain. If they do not rain, then one should bathe them with liquor and heat them with a fire of *khadira* wood; then they will rain. If they still do not rain, then they become afflicted with leprosy (*kuṣṭha*). This must be performed by a *vidyādhara* who partakes in the ritual feast (*kriyābhojī*). Afterwards, the rite should be withdrawn and the materials cast into a great river. (39)
May the god send rain in due season, and may there be an abundance of crops;
may the world be prosperous, and may the king be righteous.
Thus is dedication.

One who desires to stop excessive rain, because of his skill as a physician of venomous creatures, should draw forth a serpent, smear it with sandalwood, and make it drink milk. Having consecrated this with the mantra seven times, having placed it in an unbaked red jar, and having sealed it with the Great Seal (mahāmudrā), one should break the jar in the water. At that very moment, the rain will be stopped. // 41 //
One should give food to the assembly, to the disciples, and to the mantra-practitioner;
by means of food, drink, and other such offerings, the nāgas become exceedingly pleased with one who is young.
And if the ministers do not act in this manner when water is being poured, they become afflicted with leprosy as a result of their failure to satisfy the nāgas. (43)

Therefore, even kings, having bathed together with their sons and inner apartments, should drink the roots of the *pratyaṅgirā* on the fifth day of the *pratyaṅgirā* [observance] from a silver vessel, using either milk or clarified butter. Having washed that silver vessel, one should give it to a monk. For as long as a year, one will not be afraid of snakes; yet if that very snake, due to its own unwholesome karma, should bite him, then he dies. Success is achieved by reciting the mantra seven times. 44.

Alternatively, one desiring to remove leprosy should drink blood after neutralizing its poison with this mantra; it removes the leprosy. Or, having consecrated water with the root mantra, one should wash away the bite of a snake; it renders it poisonless. // 45 //

Then, one who desires to see the nāgas should empower a petal of a red lotus by reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times and cast it into a nāga lake. Thereupon, the nāgas will emerge from their courtyard and seek instructions from the practitioner, saying, "What shall we do, O Blessed One? The mantra-reciter should say whatever he desires. (46)
The fifth chapter, the ritual manual for the maṇḍala of Kurukullā.
Chapter Six

Then, when the noble youth Rāhula entered Rājagṛha for alms and, having entered, went to the Bamboo Grove, he descended into a long pond there to wash his bowl. The son of Yaśodharā was then dragged away by a *nāga*, who mistook him for a white-robed monk. At that very moment, this spell (*vidyā*) was recited by the noble youth Rāhula. As soon as it was recited, the noble youth Rāhula went into the presence of the Blessed One just as if someone had simply stepped out from their own house. Having approached, he said to the Blessed One: "Father, I have witnessed the power of that mantra which you graciously bestowed. The Blessed One asked: "Where? "From the presence of the *nāgas*. "Therefore, may the Blessed One set forth this very mantra for the protection of other living beings as well. Then, at that time, the Blessed One, having sent Vajrapāṇi, bestowed this mantra and its ritual manual (*kalpa*) upon the disciples, the bodhisattvas, and the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. "Therefore, O sons of good family, for whoever recites this mantra and its ritual manual after having made a mandala with sandalwood, there shall be no danger of poisoning or destruction by poison in their body; no fear of spiders, no fear of snakes, no fear of scabies, no fear of *nāgas*, no fear of leprosy, no fear of disease, no fear of wild beasts, no fear of deer, no fear of weapons, no fear of enemies, no fear of poverty, and no fear of untimely death. It shall not overcome them. (1)

Then the Blessed One, for the sake of protecting the Teaching, gave Hārītī, the Rākṣasī nourished by his own alms-bowl, to Mahākāla. Due to her former unwholesome karma, she was unfortunate; and because Mahākāla did not comply, he would neither stay nor take pleasure [in her], nor did he protect the Teaching. That Rākṣasī became distressed, and this *Kurukullā-kalpa* was spoken in order to bring both her and Mahākāla under control. From that time forth, she became possessed of great good fortune. Therefore, noble sons, for the sake of bringing all sentient beings under one's influence, this very mantra or its ritual manual (*kalpa*) should be practiced. // 2 //

Then a son was born to Sunanda who was handsome, pleasing, beautiful to behold, and endowed with auspicious marks, yet he was dull-witted. Then Sunanda asked the Blessed One: "Blessed One, my son has been born handsome, pleasing, beautiful to behold, and endowed with auspicious marks, yet he is dull-witted. How then, Blessed One, can his wisdom increase? If, Blessed One, this child were to become literate, then he would enter into your teaching. Having heard this, the Blessed One established mindful presence before him and spoke this ritual (*kalpa*) and this mantra. As soon as it was spoken, that son of Sunanda, named Rohiṇīkumāra, became possessed of wisdom. Within twelve years, he became proficient in all treatises and mastered all arts and crafts. Therefore, noble sons, for the sake of increasing great wisdom, one should train in this very mantra or its ritual. // 3 //
The sixth chapter: The Nidāna-kalpa of Kurukullā.
Chapter 7. Then the Blessed One spoke to Khecarasiddhi.
Having properly taken the mercury, free from defects such as those caused by the mountains,
and having placed it within a cavity in a stone, one should rub it with the Lord of the World.
Furthermore, having washed it with the juices of medicinal herbs, one should likewise rub it for three days with the juice of *yavatiktikā* and also with the juice of *ākhukarṇī*.

One should grind [the substance] with the milk of a barren woman, a crow-hawk, the sun-plant (*bhāskara*), and the thunderbolt-plant (*vajra*), along with water from the ear of one whose ears have not been pierced, mixed with breast milk. // 3 //
Having washed that mercury even seven times with sour gruel (kāñjika), one should rub it,
place it in an iron vessel, and cook it in a decoction of *vṛddhadāraka* and *vaṭa*.
One should indeed cause the gold flowers to be rolled by the assistant with a lump of clay, alternating between the lower and upper parts,
for one hundred thousand recitations of the root mantra.
A stone, consecrated by that mantra and by the Gandhasūrya [mantra],
should be dissolved in fire within an iron vessel through the application of powder.
When the stone has become somewhat worn, one should swallow the entire *khapattra*;
thereafter, one should take gold, and then again the *mākṣika* of that very same [substance]. (7)
Then, one should digest silver and copper, as well as five parts of steel;
one should digest all of this sixfold times, and it will become equal in luster to the sun.
The wise man should pierce clusters [of targets] with its twang;
having pierced a *palaka* with a *māṣa*-weight arrow, he knows the *sūtaka* (mercury) has been perfected. // 9 //
Having cleansed the diamond with the milky sap of *snuhī* mixed with *meṣaśṛṅgī*,
one should age the diamond in the perfected mercury using substances derived from the body of a *chucchundarī*.
When the mercury has been bound by this [method], one should digest cinnabar and the like;
the knower of the yoga of Kurukullā should always digest pearl with his own gaze. 11.
One should always take a mere grain [of this substance]; it makes a woman desire a hundred men.
By using it for seven nights, the practitioner shall attain the power of moving through the sky.
The Rasakhecarasiddhitantra.

Having made a paste with mercury, one should place it in a crucible made from the seeds of the *bakula* tree; then, one should heat it in a red-robe crucible (*raktakañcukī-mūṣā*) or in a small furnace (*lohikā*). // 13 //
For there is no doubt that death awaits Vaṅga when it is processed with its own flux;
however, having dissolved that [Vaṅga] in one *pala* of silver, one should then [dissolve it] again in sixty *palas*.
One may pierce even mountains and create a mountain of light;
through the *tāra* [mantra], the accomplishment of *tāra* shall arise, and by means of it, one shall attain the welfare of sentient beings. // 15 //
From the welfare of sentient beings comes the accumulation of merit; from that accumulation comes supreme enlightenment. // 16 //
Thus ends the Tārasiddhi Tantra.
As for the blue *kroṇṇa* as it has been described, it is called the "blue-spotted" (*nīlacitraka*);
by drinking that with milk, a practitioner becomes one who lives for a thousand years within a month. (17)
Having consecrated a black Kalambikā plant with mantras and placed it in a vessel of milk, the yogi should consume it on the eighth lunar day; he shall live as long as the sun and moon endure.
Having obtained *haridrābhrāmarī*, one should stir it with milk and drink it;
if one drinks it while observing the *poṣadha* fast, one shall be free from wrinkles and gray hair. (19)
The lifespan of those who are the Ministers of Brahmā (Brahmapurohitas), wherever they may reside, shall likewise be like that of the fruit of the banyan tree; of this there is no doubt. (20)
Having taken the form of a crab and stirred it with milk, one should drink it;
if the ritual is performed on a *poṣadha* day, one shall be free from wrinkles and grey hair. (21)
Thus ends the Rasāyanasiddhitantra.
The seventh [chapter]: The Ritual Manual for the Alchemical Elixir of Kurukullā.
Chapter 8.
Then the Blessed One spoke on the applications of medicinal herbs:
A son, observing a vow, should mix the flowers of the *baka* tree with milk and drink them.
His wife too, having observed the poṣadha vow, should drink [it]; she shall give birth to an excellent and fortunate son. // 1 //
Those women who, being observant of the poṣadha vows, drink the vacā fruits ground with milk while reciting this mantra, shall obtain a son endowed with the marks of a king. // 2 //

She who drinks the root of the *lakṣaṇākṣa* with milk from the remains of her bath shall obtain a noble son—one whose form is perfected by the white mustard seed (*siddhārtha*), whose body is complete, and who is made proficient through both sword and scripture. // 3 //
Having uprooted the root of the *jalaśītalā* plant and placed it within the hair,
once empowered with seven recitations of the mantra, that very [remedy] shall destroy even a chronic fever in an instant.
A yogi who takes the root of *kanaka* and places it upon the hair of one afflicted by quartan fever, or seized by other fevers, shall drive away those fevers.
Sulphur, the smoke of burnt salt, and fermented gruel, combined with the juice of the *dvirepharāja* (the "king of bees," i.e., the *bhr̥ṅgarāja*),
ground into a paste and placed in a copper vessel, brings about the destruction of glass.
Having uprooted the root of the white *uccaṭa* plant and ground it with milk, one should drink as much as desired;
by means of this mantra, recited fifty times, the male organ of men shall become excellent and erect. (7)

For the earth is well known by the name "Nāgā," and when she is milked into the *liṅga*, she produces semen endowed with strength that generates progeny, provided she has been consecrated fifty times with this mantra. (8)
For one who has not yet cut his teeth, [one should apply] gorocana, lolā, and the roots of nṛparāja under an auspicious lunar mansion;
with that, a tilaka should be made in the middle of the forehead, which is effective for bringing the three worlds under one's control.

Having taken the eyes, the heart, the flesh of the forehead, and likewise the nose of a dead person, one should grind them and cook them in oil under the Puṣya asterism; this makes people subject to one's will.
With the collyrium from the head of the king of serpents—known as *śukra*, *rakta*, and *kusuma*—those whose eyes are anointed with that collyrium bring the queen of kings under their control. (11)
If one recites this mantra fifty times and places one's feet upon the ground,
they will know all treasures situated in the earth merely by the movement of those two feet.
If a vein throbs in the foot and moves upward,
the perfected ones (siddhas) declare that wealth exists at a distance;
this occurs when the sensation is preceded by a sound as if saying, "Where there is wealth."
The Vidyādhara must look upon the surface of the earth. // 13 //
By merely applying a plaster of powdered musk-shrew mixed with bdellium,
one travels easily on a path made impassable by rutting elephants.
Anointed with ghee produced from the milk of an exceedingly black female dog, he walks upon sandals made of camel-hide and wanders in the water. (15)
If one hides Piṅgala, Saṃkucaka, Kaṇṭa, Gṛhamadhya, Gopya, Kallabāla, and Madirānāśa within the house, it brings prosperity; by uprooting them, it becomes auspicious. // 16 //
It is not surprising that fire does not burn when wood struck by a thunderbolt is thrown into a potter’s kiln; yet it burns again when sprinkled with wine. (17)
Having recited the mantra over the price and empowered it for the sake of those seeking wealth, the yogi made the sale; thus, the merchants became exceedingly wealthy. (18)
By throwing monkey excrement into the seed-vessel, the liquor reaches destruction;
by smearing it with water from the leaves of the *varuṇa* tree, that vessel becomes fit once again. (19)
By sprinkling water with *bakula* leaves, the mothers become well-disposed;
likewise, they are pacified by incense made from *bhūtakeśa* and by those who are clad in saffron robes.
A child who has vomited milk will become healthy again by smearing the ashes of a peacock’s tail on the throat, through the power of this supreme yoga. (21)
When prepared according to the prescribed ritual and inscribed upon a sheet of lead,
these word-armors (padakavaca) bring about the destruction of imprisonment and the fear of weapons when placed within the mouth or the belly.
All the *piṇḍas* should be joined with the syllables *kṣa*, *ma*, *ra*, and *ya*, and adorned with the syllable *e*.
At the end of the *padakas* and the *kavacas*, the wise one should employ the four *aṇḍas*.

The letter *ai* is the single *bindu*; *ka*, *ṣa*, and *ta* situated at the end of the sixth class (*ṣa*); the seed-syllable of Vāyu, which is the *arandhra*, surrounded by fire, with its head marked by the *bindu* and the void;
from the fiery [seed] comes the *tavarga*, followed by the protracted (*pluta*) vowel, and finally all the letters standing at the summit.
These certainly bring about supreme success even without the application of [specific] methods. // 24 //
This conjunction is one whose efficacy has been directly perceived.
Having given seven sprinklings with water from the Daṇḍotpala, Aśara-puṅkha, Nicūla, Girikarṇikā, and Toya plants, the wise one should write [the mantra] upon a sheet of lead.
The perfected great mantra destroys the binding of shackles and fetters, the raining down of weapons in battle, and the ill-will of others as well. (26)
Having placed the knowledge on his arm and having inscribed the king of mantras, he becomes as wealthy as Kubera, possessing inexhaustible riches and remaining invincible. (27)
By touching the alms-bowl with this mantra, "Oṃ Kurukulle svāhā," a monk obtains food as alms even in a region of extreme famine. // 28 //
If a woman drinks utpala tubers and kaśeru roots stirred with milk, she will certainly stabilize her pregnancy; that rite may even be performed by herself. (29)
If a woman grinds the five fruits of the Magadha region and drinks them with milk, she will give birth with ease through the power of this mantra. (30)
A woman who grinds the leaves of *nimba* and *vāruṇa* with "thunderbolt water" (*vajrodaka*) and applies an ointment to the vagina will give birth to her children easily and with comfort. (31)
Gajamāgadhikā with vacā, hayagandhā, and buffalo butter—this formulation combined with hair brings about growth when used for the purpose of enlarging the breasts. (32)
The yoga joined with the fruit of the *kumbhāṇḍī* brings about success in the practice of the root-mantra.
He who eats all food [prepared] in this way, or drinks water through the nose, being one whose soul is united with the mantra-yoga, arrests the "untimely ripening" (*akālapāka*) of the head. (33)
The root of *avasanikā*, combined with the seeds of *kākamācī* and *kanaka*, ground with camphor water and applied as an ointment to the genitals, causes thick women to flow [with desire]. // 34 //
This ointment causes her to cease from undying passion, so that she does not dwell with her husband nor show him respect; it even brings about his death, for the sake of her own departure. (35)
Having lit a lamp in a vessel of hog’s oil during sexual union,
even a person who is quick to climax shall remain for a long time upon the woman’s hips.
When the house is being consumed by vajra-fire, those men who sprinkle liquor with mantras extinguish the fire; this is the yoga proclaimed by the Lord of the World. // 37 //
Now, there is also another application.

Having drawn a ten-petaled lotus in the center of a moon disc, and having written "Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture svāhā" on the tip of each petal, one should write "Devadatta, bring [him] under control! within the syllable *tāṃ* at the hub. One should also encircle that syllable *tāṃ* with the mantra: "Oṃ aḥ Kurukulle, bring Devadatta under control, hrīḥ. Outside the moon disc, one should encircle it with the mantra: "Oṃ Prasannatāre, O gracious one, O you who cause grace, bring Devadatta under control, hrīḥ. Furthermore, outside of this, one should draw a sixteen-petaled lotus and encircle each petal with the mantra: "Oṃ Prasannatāre, O gracious one, O you who cause grace, hrīḥ, make Devadatta submissive, hrīḥ. Finally, one should encircle the entire diagram from the outside with sixteen syllables. Having written this on birch bark with lac, yellow orpiment, red sandalwood, saffron, and camphor, and having wrapped it in beeswax, one should place it in the "three sweets" (honey, ghee, and sugar) and worship it at the three junctions of the day with red offerings. There is no doubt that he will become submissive. // 38 //
Now, there is yet another application:

having drawn a sixteen-petaled lotus, one should write on each petal—*a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aṃ aḥ*—and in the central pericarp, *oṃ haḥ kurukulle devadattaṃ vaśam ānaya haḥ svāhā*. One should surround the outside of the lotus with three rows of *oṃ* syllables. [The person] becomes submissive; of this there is no doubt. // 39 //

Thus spoke the Protector, standing in the midst of the assembly. And those beings who were on Potalaka, the king of mountains—the Blessed One, who suffers with the suffering of others—there is nothing that the Buddhas, the perfected ones who act for the benefit of sentient beings, do not necessarily perform. This conduct is not unprecedented; it is not lost, but rather they have once again brought about our upliftment. 40.

The Blessed One said this, and the Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas Avalokiteśvara and the rest, as well as the entire assembly—including gods, humans, asuras, garuḍas, and gandharvas—rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had spoken. // 41 //
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the Kurukullā-kalpa, of the glorious Bhagavatī Ārya Tārā.
The *Āryakurukullākalpa* is completed. It was extracted from the *Tārodbhava*, which is included within the *Tārārṇavamahāyogatantra*.
